synopsis: Open-source simulation is viable as a low-license-cost core, but not the lowest-total-cost option: coupling, assets, scenario databases and validation evidence still require engineering and maintenance [f196, f8296, f8303]. The booklet judges compute cheap relative to engineering labor, estimates a labor floor of roughly USD 150,000–260,000 per specialist per year, and warns that even free-software programs can cost seven figures annually [f198, f13550, f13551]. On-road precedents demonstrate substantial resource commitments—PEGASUS ran January 2016–June 2019 with about EUR 34.5 million and 1,791 person-months, while VVM ran July 2019–June 2023 with EUR 47 million—but no public study supplies team size, timeline or total cost for an off-highway build-versus-buy decision [f1204, f1205, f8314]. Direct job-site creation costs, off-road labeling costs, and independently published off-road compute costs and return on investment remain missing; tool budgets therefore need vendor quotations rather than published benchmarks [f3847, f5424, f10615, f8308]. Vehicle-in-the-loop is emerging and capital-intensive, its economic justification for this program remains uncertain, and it is recommended only where extra physical fidelity warrants the investment [f338, f1119, f550]. Planning should quantify money and scarce engineering capacity, address ownership, budgets and licences after September 2027, and avoid counting physical-test substitution savings before they are earned; until simulator trust is established, dual simulator-and-physical-test costs are an explicit inference [f10273, f10179, f10510, f10511].
